WASHINGTON (CNN) -- A distraught, sobbing Afghan Taliban member begged the court for mercy, but got none as an unmoved federal judge here Monday handed down maximum life sentences for convictions on drug trafficking and narco-terrorism charges. A guard watches over a pile of burning drugs in Kabul, Afghanistan, on June 25, 2008. Khan Mohammed, 38, of Nangarhar Province became the first person convicted and sentenced in the United States under a 2006 law that increased the penalty for a defendant found to be involved  with terrorism and distributing illegal drugs. Mohammed, who had been extradited from Afghanistan, was convicted by a jury in May of plotting a rocket attack on U.S. military forces and Afghan civilians at Jalalabad Airfield. He also was found guilty of distributing between $1 million and $3 million worth of heroin into the United States "to kill Americans as part of a jihad." Mohammed's court-appointed lawyer, conceding that "what he did was wrong," urged U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly to be lenient and sentence his client to only 20 years in prison. Then the full-bearded Mohammed, dressed in an orange jailhouse jumpsuit, addressed the judge. With tears streaming down his face, and choking back his words, he begged for only one or two years. "I have little children and a woman. They depend on me," Mohammed began. "I'm so worried about them." His lengthy emotional appeal went on to include his reason for selling opium. "In my village that's how you have to make a living. There is no house there without opium," he said. Justice Department prosecutor Matthew Stiglitz, however, urged the court to "send a message of deterrence," and warned against "the confluence of drug trafficking and terrorism." "No, he's not the Osama bin Laden of terrorism. No, he's not the Pablo Escobar of the drug world," Stiglitz told the judge. "But this is where the rubber meets the road." Bin Laden is the head of al Qaeda, while Escobar, who died in 1993, was the most powerful of Colombian drug lords. "Afghanistan is ground zero for opium, and an almost limitless source of funds to the Taliban," he argued. Kollar-Kotelly agreed fully with the prosecutors, and strongly admonished the Taliban defendant. "You were convicted 99 percent by your own words," the judge declared, as she recalled how a "courageous" Afghan police chief wore an undercover wire to record Mohammed's plotting. "The fact that no one died is only because you didn't get the missiles you wanted," she said. "In 2006, you celebrated the Americans' use of the opium. It was a jihad. You knew the damage it could cause," the judge continued. "Because of your undiluted hatred for the United States, you might well have launched other attacks had you not been arrested." She added, "Terrorists stand unique among criminals. Deterrence is very important here." Then, concluding dramatically, the judge turned directly to the defendant. "I heard your concerns for your family but no acceptance of responsibility for your action," the judge said. "Defendants often express worry for their families, but if they considered the consequences of their actions beforehand, maybe they would have acted differently."

WASHINGTON (CNN) — An Afghan Taliban member, visibly devastated and crying, pleaded with a federal court for mercy on Monday, but the judge showed no leniency, imposing the maximum punishment of life in prison for his convictions on drug-trafficking and narco-terrorism charges.

Khan Mohammed, 38, from Afghanistan’s Nangarhar Province, became the first person to be convicted and sentenced in the United States under a 2006 statute that raised penalties for defendants found to have links to both terrorism and the distribution of illegal drugs. Mohammed had been extradited from Afghanistan.

In May, a jury found him guilty of planning a rocket attack against U.S. military personnel and Afghan civilians at Jalalabad Airfield. He was also convicted of trafficking heroin worth between $1 million and $3 million into the United States, with the stated aim of killing Americans as part of a jihad.

A court-appointed attorney for Mohammed acknowledged that “what he did was wrong,” but asked U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly to show leniency and give his client a 20-year prison term instead of life.

Mohammed, wearing an orange jail uniform and a full beard, then spoke directly to the judge. Crying openly and struggling to speak, he asked to be sentenced to only one or two years behind bars.

“I have little children and a woman. They depend on me,” he said. “I’m so worried about them.”

During his extended emotional plea, Mohammed also explained why he had sold opium. “In my village that’s how you have to make a living. There is no house there without opium,” he told the court.

But Justice Department prosecutor Matthew Stiglitz asked the judge to impose a sentence that would “send a message of deterrence,” warning of the danger created by the merging of narcotics trafficking and terrorism.

“No, he’s not the Osama bin Laden of terrorism. No, he’s not the Pablo Escobar of the drug world,” Stiglitz said. “But this is where the rubber meets the road.”

Osama bin Laden was the leader of al Qaeda, while Pablo Escobar, who died in 1993, was once Colombia’s most powerful drug lord.

Stiglitz argued that Afghanistan was “ground zero for opium” and that the trade provided the Taliban with an almost unlimited supply of money.

Judge Kollar-Kotelly accepted the prosecution’s position and sharply criticized Mohammed. She said his conviction was based overwhelmingly on his own statements, noting that a “courageous” Afghan police chief had secretly recorded Mohammed while wearing an undercover wire.

“You were convicted 99 percent by your own words,” she said.

The judge added that the only reason no one was killed was because Mohammed never obtained the missiles he had sought.

“In 2006, you celebrated the Americans’ use of the opium. It was a jihad. You knew the damage it could cause,” Kollar-Kotelly said. She also stated that, because of Mohammed’s “undiluted hatred for the United States,” he might have carried out additional attacks if he had not been arrested.

“Terrorists stand unique among criminals,” she said. “Deterrence is very important here.”

Turning to Mohammed at the end of the hearing, the judge said she had listened to his worries about his family but had not heard him take responsibility for his conduct.

“Defendants often express worry for their families,” she said, “but if they considered the consequences of their actions beforehand, maybe they would have acted differently.”

**Afghan Taliban member sentenced to life in U.S. prison for narco-terrorism**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Khan Mohammed, an Afghan Taliban member convicted of trafficking heroin and opium to fund attacks against U.S. forces, was sentenced in federal court in Washington to life in prison, U.S. officials said.

Mohammed was convicted under a 2006 U.S. narco-terrorism law that allows prosecutors to target drug trafficking tied to terrorist activity. Authorities said his case marked one of the first major uses of the statute against a Taliban-linked defendant brought to the United States for trial.

Prosecutors alleged that Mohammed conspired to sell large quantities of narcotics, including heroin and opium, knowing the proceeds would help support Taliban operations and attacks against American and coalition troops in Afghanistan.

Federal officials described the case as part of a broader effort to disrupt the financial networks that sustain terrorist organizations.

“This prosecution demonstrates that those who traffic drugs to fund terrorism can be brought to justice in U.S. courts,” officials said at the time of the sentencing.

Mohammed was captured in Afghanistan and later transferred to the United States, where he stood trial in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. A jury found him guilty of drug trafficking and narco-terrorism charges.

The 2006 law was designed to close gaps in U.S. counterterrorism and narcotics enforcement by making it a crime to engage in drug trafficking with the intent or knowledge that the proceeds would support terrorist activity.

Afghanistan has long been the world’s leading producer of opium, and U.S. officials have said Taliban factions have relied on profits from the drug trade to finance insurgent operations. Mohammed’s conviction underscored the Justice Department’s strategy of treating narcotics trafficking and terrorism financing as intertwined threats.

He will serve his life sentence in the federal prison system.

Prosecutors described Mohammed as someone who viewed the drug trade as a source of revenue for insurgent violence. They argued that his conduct demonstrated the connection between Afghanistan’s opium economy and militant activity, particularly in regions where insurgent groups have relied on narcotics profits for funding.

At sentencing, the court imposed a life term, emphasizing the seriousness of using drug proceeds to support terrorism. U.S. officials said the conviction sent a message that traffickers who use narcotics money to fund attacks on Americans or allied forces can be prosecuted in American courts, even when the conduct occurs overseas.

The narco-terrorism statute was designed to target individuals who traffic drugs while knowing or intending that the activity will benefit terrorist organizations or terrorist acts.
